title: Jeremiah 25:15–29
context: Jeremiah reports the LORD’s command, “Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand,” and his own response, taking the cup and making the nations drink, beginning with Jerusalem and Judah and moving through Egypt, the Philistine cities, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, the peoples of Arabia, Elam, the Medes, and the kings of the north, with “the king of Sheshach” drinking last. The image of the cup appears elsewhere (cf. Ps 75:8; Isa 51:17), and the place names are identified with varying confidence, while Sheshach is commonly read as a name for Babylon in light of 51:41. Both traditions share the ground that God’s judgment begins with his own people and reaches all nations, and how the LORD works “evil” on the city called by his name points to the existing box at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: For the LORD, the God of Israel, says to me: “Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand, and cause all the nations to whom I send you to drink it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says to Jeremiah, “Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand, and cause all the nations to whom I send you to drink it.” Arminian readers note the vivid image of judgment as a cup to be drunk.

The cup is a picture, and how it was enacted is not described.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the cup as an image of God’s righteous judgment (cf. Ps 75:8; Isa 51:17).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God’s wrath is just.

verses.text: They will drink, and reel back and forth, and be insane, because of the sword that I will send among them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will drink, and reel back and forth, and be insane, because of the sword that I will send among them.” Arminian readers note that the cup’s effects are tied to the coming sword.

The drunkenness pictures the confusion of war.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the image as the disorientation of nations under judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry about real historical judgment, not as a literal drinking scene, while affirming God’s rule over war.

verses.text: Then I took the cup at the LORD’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, to whom the LORD had sent me:
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says, “Then I took the cup at the LORD’s hand, and made all the nations to drink.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s obedience to a hard commission.

How this was carried out is not described.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet acting as God’s messenger, whose word carries God’s sentence.

Shared ground: both traditions read the action as prophetic proclamation rather than speculating on a literal journey to each nation.

verses.text: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, with its kings and its princes, to make them a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing, and a curse, as it is today;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list begins with “Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, with its kings and its princes.” Arminian readers note that judgment starts with God’s own people.

The phrase “as it is today” may reflect a later vantage point, though this is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see judgment beginning at the house of God (cf. 1 Pet 4:17).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that covenant privilege brings greater accountability, not exemption.

verses.text: Pharaoh king of Egypt, with his servants, his princes, and all his people;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Pharaoh king of Egypt, with his servants, his princes, and all his people.” Arminian readers note that Egypt, which Judah often trusted, is under the same cup.

Judah’s political hopes cannot save it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s sovereignty over the great powers of the day.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that no nation is outside God’s judgment, and both note Egypt’s role elsewhere in Jeremiah (cf. ch. 46).

verses.text: and all the mixed people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, all the kings of the Philistines, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list includes “all the mixed people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, all the kings of the Philistines.” Arminian readers note the reach of the judgment to many peoples.

The locations of some names, such as Uz, are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the wide scope of God’s rule.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list as a survey of nations around Judah, hedging identifications and noting that Ashdod is called a “remnant.”

verses.text: Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon.” Arminian readers note that Judah’s eastern neighbors are named together.

Each receives its own oracle later in the book (cf. chs. 48–49).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s dealings with these neighboring nations.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that these nations are accountable to God, while the later oracles are named rather than harmonized with this list.

verses.text: and all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the isle which is beyond the sea;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with “all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the isle which is beyond the sea.” Arminian readers note the coastal and maritime powers.

The “isle” is not identified in the text.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the reach of God’s judgment to distant lands.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list as showing that even trading powers far from Judah stand under God’s rule.

verses.text: Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who have the corners of their beard cut off;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who have the corners of their beard cut off.” Arminian readers note peoples of the desert regions.

The last phrase may describe a custom of certain tribes, though its exact meaning is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the inclusion of peoples on the edges of Judah’s world.

Shared ground: both traditions hedge the identifications and agree that the point is the universal scope of the cup.

verses.text: and all the kings of Arabia, all the kings of the mixed people who dwell in the wilderness;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with “all the kings of Arabia, all the kings of the mixed people who dwell in the wilderness.” Arminian readers note the inclusion of desert peoples.

The list continues to widen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s rule over peoples near and far.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the survey of nations, without pressing exact identifications.

verses.text: and all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with “all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes.” Arminian readers note the turn toward the east.

Zimri is not securely identified.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the scope reaching to distant powers (cf. 49:34–39 on Elam).

Shared ground: both traditions hedge the identification of Zimri and read the list as showing God’s rule over the nations.

verses.text: and all the kings of the north, far and near, one with another; and all the kingdoms of the world, which are on the surface of the earth. The king of Sheshach will drink after them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list closes with “all the kings of the north, far and near, one with another; and all the kingdoms of the world.” Arminian readers note the climax of the list.

“The king of Sheshach will drink after them” is commonly read as referring to Babylon (cf. 51:41).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Babylon drinking last, after serving as the instrument of judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the empire that judges others will itself be judged, as 25:12 already said.

verses.text: “You shall tell them, ‘The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Drink, and be drunk, vomit, fall, and rise no more, because of the sword which I will send among you.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Jeremiah to say, “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says,” and then commands the nations to “Drink, and be drunk, vomit, fall, and rise no more.” Arminian readers note the severity of the image.

It is tied to “the sword which I will send.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the strong language as prophetic poetry about real defeat in war, and both handle it soberly.

verses.text: It shall be, if they refuse to take the cup at your hand to drink, then you shall tell them, ‘The LORD of Armies says: “You shall surely drink.
verses.arminianNotes:
“It shall be, if they refuse to take the cup at your hand to drink.” Arminian readers note that refusal does not avert the judgment.

The LORD says, “You shall surely drink.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of God’s decree of judgment on the nations.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that human resistance cannot overturn God’s righteous judgment, while 26:3 shows that repentance is a different matter.

verses.text: For, behold, I begin to work evil at the city which is called by my name; and should you be utterly unpunished? You will not be unpunished; for I will call for a sword on all the inhabitants of the earth, says the LORD of Armies.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I begin to work evil at the city which is called by my name; and should you be utterly unpunished?” Arminian readers take “evil” here as calamity or disaster.

If Jerusalem is judged, the nations cannot expect exemption.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read “evil” as judgment rather than moral wrong, and see God governing it.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God is not the author of sin.
